prompt: 80% of a program can be spread perfectly across cores; the rest is serial. What is the speedup on 4 cores? Use fixed-work Amdahl assumptions: equal core speeds and no added parallel overhead.

options.explanation: That assumes 100% parallel code. The serial 20% still takes the same time.
This multiplies 0.8 × 4. Amdahl's law divides the time instead.
Correct. The new time is 0.2 + 0.8 / 4 = 0.4 of the original, so the speedup is 1 / 0.4 = 2.5.
5× is the limit with infinitely many cores, 1 / 0.2.

workedExample:
Amdahl's law: the serial part keeps its time and the parallel part divides over the cores.

```formula
S(n) = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / n)
S(4) = 1 / ((1 − 0.8) + 0.8 / 4)
S(4) = 1 / (0.2 + 0.2) = 1 / 0.4
S(4) = 2.5
S_max = 1 / (1 − 0.8) = 5
where
S(n): the speedup on n cores, original time divided by new time
n: the number of equally fast cores, 4 here
p: the parallel fraction of the original run time, 0.8
1 − p: the serial fraction, 0.2, which more cores cannot shorten
S_max: the ceiling with infinitely many cores, when the parallel part shrinks to nothing
In words: the run takes 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4 of its old time on 4 cores, a speedup of 2.5, and can never beat 5.
```

prompt: A data-processing job is 95% parallelisable. You can buy a 16-core or a 64-core server. What speedups does Amdahl's law predict, and what is the ceiling? Assume equal per-core speed, fixed work and no parallel overhead; p is the fraction of original single-core execution time.

options.explanation: This ignores the serial 5%, which takes the same time however many cores there are.
This multiplies the core count by 0.95, which is not how Amdahl's law works.

options.text: About 9.1× and 9.1×; more cores never help
options.explanation: More cores do help, just with diminishing returns: 64 cores are about 1.7× better than 16 here.

options.text: About 9.1× and 15.4×, with a ceiling of 20×

workedExample:
Apply Amdahl's law with p = 0.95:

```formula
S(n) = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / n)
S(16) = 1 / (0.05 + 0.95 / 16) ≈ 9.14
S(64) = 1 / (0.05 + 0.95 / 64) ≈ 15.4
S_max = 1 / 0.05 = 20
where
S(n): the speedup on n equally fast cores
n: the number of cores, 16 or 64
p: the parallel fraction of the original single-core run time, 0.95
S_max: the ceiling as the number of cores grows without limit: 1 / (1 − p)
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the serial 5% caps the speedup at 20, so 16 cores give about 9.1 and 64 cores only about 15.4.
```

1. Quadrupling the cores improves speedup only by 15.4 / 9.14 ≈ 1.7×.
2. If the same workload could instead have parallelisable fraction 97.5%, the ideal ceiling would be 1 / 0.025 = 40×. Whether that change is feasible or cost-effective needs separate evidence.
